items.context: Whining in your ear at bedtime.

img.author: CDC/ Amy E. Lockwood, MS
img.alt: A slim black-and-white striped insect with long legs on a green leaf.

items.why: An Aedes mosquito with its striped legs and slender body.
items.pearl: Only female mosquitoes bite; they need blood to make eggs. Males sip nectar.

items.context: Lurking in a corner of the shed.

img.author: CDC/ M. Parsons
img.alt: A shiny black spider with a round abdomen hanging in a web.

items.why: A black widow: glossy black with a round abdomen, related to Australia's redback.
items.pearl: The red hourglass is on the underside. Our redback wears its red stripe on the back instead.

items.context: In a bowl on the kitchen bench.

img.author: CDC/ Amanda Mills (cropped)
img.alt: Shiny round dark red fruit piled in a white bowl.

items.pearl: Cut a grape almost in half, microwave it and it can make a spark of glowing plasma. Please don't try it at home.

img.author: CDC/ Dr. Henry D. Pratt
img.alt: A grey, papery structure covered in six-sided cells.

items.why: A paper wasp nest, built from chewed wood fibre into six-sided cells.
items.pearl: Wasps invented paper long before people did: they chew wood and mix it with saliva.

items.context: Sunbaking on a rock in a pond.

img.author: CDC/ Eric Grafman (cropped)
img.alt: A domed dark shell with yellow-striped skin and a pointed head.

items.why: A red-eared slider turtle with its striped head and domed shell.
items.pearl: In Australia it's a declared invasive pest. If you see one in the wild, report it.

items.context: Coiled up and not happy about it.

img.author: CDC/ Harold George Scott, PhD (cropped)
img.alt: Patterned scales in brown and black chevrons ending in a segmented tail tip.

items.why: A timber rattlesnake: chevron-patterned scales and a segmented rattle on the tail.
items.pearl: A new rattle segment is added each time the snake sheds, not once a year, so you can't count them to get its age.

items.context: Pouring out of a crack in the floorboards.

img.author: CDC
img.alt: A crowd of tiny pale insects with dark wings lined up along a gap in pale timber.

items.why: A swarm of winged termites leaving the colony to start new ones.
items.pearl: In the Northern Territory, magnetic termites build flat mounds that all point north–south to manage the heat.

items.context: Electron microscope view, about 100 times life size, with some cat fur.

img.author: CDC/ Callie Carr (cropped)
img.alt: A grey electron microscope image of a rounded, pitted body with hairs across it.

items.why: A swollen tick, still attached, seen under an electron microscope among strands of cat fur.
items.pearl: Ticks aren't insects. They have eight legs and are related to spiders.

img.author: CDC/ Harold G. Scott (cropped)
img.alt: A fat green body covered in clusters of fine spines.

items.why: An Io moth caterpillar, bristling with green stinging spines.
items.pearl: The adult Io moth flashes two huge eyespots on its back wings to startle birds.

items.context: Electron microscope view, about 24 times life size.

img.author: CDC/ William L. Nicholson, Ph.D.; Cal Welbourn, Ph.D., Gary R. Mullen (cropped)
img.alt: A grey electron microscope image of a scaly limb ending in thin clawed toes.

items.why: A small lizard's foot, armoured in scales, with clawed toes.
items.pearl: Lizard scales are made of keratin, the same protein as your fingernails.
